Line 213: BACKUP: '##### 3.	In older Menaia, which our Menaia also follow, troparia and kontakia are not given to every Saint, but in closer times we find them given in our Horologia. Therefore one should not wonder if regarding the use of troparia at the Hours the rubrics in some way do not agree with the Menaion and our Horologion or Prayer Book. For when a Saint had a troparion and kontakion, according to the ancient Typikon, they were taken at all Hours; but according to the Typikon of our Horologions and Prayer Books, in order not to repeat at all Hours on all days one and the same troparion and kontakion, for a certain variety at the 1st Hour - the troparion and kontakion of the day of the week, at the 3rd and 9th - of the Saint, and at the 6th - of the Temple.'

The designation of a saint "on 4" or "on 6" depends on the number of troparia in each Ode of his Canon at Matins. There are three cases of a Saint without Polyeleos: that is, there may occur only one saint on 4, or two on 4, or one on 6. When we say one or two saints, we understand them as having separate services, for there may be several saints [commemorated], but they have only one service. The ecclesiastical rubric does not provide for more than two services to saints [on one day][^45].')

Line 123: BACKUP: '##### 7.	If there be several Prokimena, Alleluias, Apostle-Gospels and Communion Hymns, then one must know how to take them. Know first, that in church typikons more than two are not given, with the exception of Apostle-Gospels, of which only in Slavonic typikons three are given, for the Slavs are richer in supplications than the Greeks. For where three readings coincide, the Greek typikons do not give the sequential one, but the Slavonic ones take it under the refrain of the first reading, as if one with it[^94]. When this is impossible, on the occasion of some great feast, then they order to take it on the day before under the refrain with the sequential one[^95]. However, this rule has been preserved among us perhaps only in cathedral churches, for in others usually only one Apostle-Gospel is taken, as also one service either of the day, or of the saint, or one for need. If, therefore, there be two Prokimena and two Alleluias, then both are taken under one heading, that is both Prokimena - before the refrain of the first reading, both Alleluias - after the completion of the second reading. However, the first Prokimenon is taken twice, namely: once - before and once - after the verse, the second - only once and without a verse, for in this case the Typikon does not give a verse. Similarly also "Alleluia": both of its verses are taken only of the first service, and of the second - only one first verse[^96]. The Heading, that is from whom: from Paul, from Matthew or from another, is taken only of the first reading, and the others usually are not taken, although it would be better to announce the headings of other readings as well, for it is not indifferent to the listeners to know the reading of which holy author is being proclaimed; and for this reason only would the rubric make certain sense, which orders to take the sequential reading under the refrain, for taking one reading under the refrain of another means merging it with the previous one because its heading is not announced. If the heading of the following third reading, which is not taken under the refrain, is not named, then it should have been said that this third reading is also taken under the refrain. "Let us be attentive" is announced only at the beginning of the first reading. If there be two Communion Hymns, then "Alleluia" is repeated only upon the completion of the second[^97].'

Line 242: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 7.	If there be several Prokimena, Alleluias, Apostle-Gospels and Communion Hymns, then one must know how to take them. Know first, that in church typikons more than two are not given, with the exception of Apostle-Gospels, of which only in Slavonic typikons three are given, for the Slavs are richer in supplications than the Greeks. For where three readings coincide, the Greek typikons do not give the sequential one, but the Slavonic ones take it under the refrain of the first reading, as if one with it[^94]. When this is impossible, on the occasion of some great feast, then they order to take it on the day before under the refrain with the sequential one[^95]. However, this rule has been preserved among us perhaps only in cathedral churches, for in others usually only one Apostle-Gospel is taken, as also one service either of the day, or of the saint, or one for need. If, therefore, there be two Prokimena and two Alleluias, then both are taken under one heading, that is both Prokimena - before the refrain of the first reading, both Alleluias - after the completion of the second reading. However, the first Prokimenon is taken twice, namely: once - before and once - after the verse, the second - only once and without a verse, for in this case the Typikon does not give a verse. Similarly also "Alleluia": both of its verses are taken only of the first service, and of the second - only one first verse[^96]. The Heading, that is from whom: from Paul, from Matthew or from another, is taken only of the first reading, and the others usually are not taken, although it would be better to announce the headings of other readings as well, for it is not indifferent to the listeners to know the reading of which holy author is being proclaimed; and for this reason only would the rubric make certain sense, which orders to take the sequential reading under the refrain, for taking one reading under the refrain of another means merging it with the previous one because its heading is not announced. If the heading of the following third reading, which is not taken under the refrain, is not named, then it should have been said that this third reading is also taken under the refrain. "Let us be attentive" is announced only at the beginning of the first reading. If there be two Communion Hymns, then "Alleluia" is repeated only upon the completion of the second[^97].'

Line 366: BACKUP: '### 15 NOVEMBER Beginning of the Forty Days before the Nativity of Christ'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: '')
Line 369: BACKUP: '##### 1.	The fast of this Forty Days the Lviv Synod limits only to three days of each week, that is Monday, Wednesday and Friday, permitting even on those days dairy, and on other days - to eat meat, but on the condition of the 50th Psalm for the clergy, and 5 "Our Father" and 5 "Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"  for the faithful, before dinner and before supper. Our custom [is] - to adhere to the fast on the Eve of the Nativity of Christ and Theophany, even if it falls on one of the meat days; we eat nothing with dairy, or very little, until evening. Simple people abstain also from dairy and fast until evening.'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: '')
Line 371: BACKUP: '##### 2.	Regarding church services: in the first 35 days of this Forty Days the church rule prescribes a Lenten type of service with prostrations, as in Great Lent, however, only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. On other days - of the usual type. In view of the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ, which begins on 20 December, for the last five days of the Forty Days this rule does not give a Lenten service. But today with us and with the Greeks the Lenten service is limited only to Great Lent.'

         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: 'The peculiarity of the divine service of this day consists in the fact that on it is taken not only the service of the feast, or on Sunday - also the Resurrectional one, as usually happens on the Apodosis of other feasts, but the service of these two saints is also taken. The reason for this is that the service of these two saints is not transferred to another day, as happens on the Apodosis of other feasts. This can be [the case] when on the Apodosis of other feasts only one service of a saint falls, but here - two, and therefore it is not convenient to transfer it to another day, for then one would have to take three services of saints, and the church rule does not give more than two services. This transfer is all the more inconvenient because these saints have a common troparion and kontakion, although later, in Slavic editions, separate troparia were added to them.')

The reason that the Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos has a separate rule for Monday is that in this case the service of the Synaxis is combined with the service of the Sunday after the Nativity, namely of the Holy Kinsmen of God, King David, Joseph the Betrothed and James, the Brother of the Lord. If, therefore, the Synaxis falls on Monday, then the Sunday after the Nativity would fall on 1 January, that is already after the Apodosis of the Feast, which will be 31 December; therefore, according to the typikon, it is transferred back, to 26 December. We will give the rule for all three above-mentioned cases.'

Line 1945: BACKUP: '### 24 FEBRUARY First and Second Finding of the Precious Head of the Forerunner'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: '')
Line 1948: BACKUP: '##### 1.	Since the last boundary of the Triodion is 14 February, this feast always falls in the middle of the Triodion. If the Triodion is earlier, then this feast enters all the deeper into the Triodion and coincides with many Triodion services. Even more, this feast can coincide with other services, given in the Triodion from Wednesday of Meatfare Week to Tuesday of the 8th week of the Triodion, that is of the 4th of Great Lent, inclusive. The last boundary of the beginning of the Triodion is 14 February, and after subtracting from 14 February 13 days, which precede the beginning of the Triodion, 11 will remain, dividing which by 7, we will get in the quotient 1, with 4 in the remainder, that is one whole week and one not whole - the first four days; and since the first day of the first week is Sunday (for the Triodion begins on Sunday), then the first day of the second week will be Sunday, the second - Monday, the third - Tuesday, the fourth - Wednesday. And since the first Sunday of the Triodion is the Sunday of the Publican, the second - of the Prodigal [Son], the third - Meatfare, then the Wednesday on which the Finding falls will be Meatfare Wednesday (for in the Lenten Triodion the days of the week are named after the following Sunday), as the earliest boundary of this feast in relation to the Triodion. And that the last boundary of this feast in relation to the Triodion is Tuesday of the 4th week of Great Lent is proven thus. The first boundary of the Triodion is 11 January, from which to 24 February will be 45 days, dividing which by 7, we will get 6 whole weeks with a remainder of 3; but, since the first day of this remainder is Sunday, as is the first day of each of the 6 past weeks, it will be the 7th Sunday of the Triodion, and the second day will be Monday, the third - Tuesday of the 8th week of the Triodion, of the 4th of Great Lent.'
         CURRENT: '##### 4.	Yesterday's 4 stichera of the Praises of the Feast, also Glory: of the Synaxis, Both now: to the Feast.'

         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: 'This Apodosis can fall either in the middle, or outside the *Triodion*. In the middle of the *Triodion*, if the *Triodion* falls on one of 30 days from 11 January to 9 February inclusive; outside the *Triodion*, if it falls on other five days, from 10 to 14 February. And if it falls outside the *Triodion*, then the Apodosis will be 9 February, according to the general rule of the Apodosis of a feast of the Theotokos; And in this case the Afterfeast has 7 days inclusive with the Apodosis. But if it falls in the middle of the *Triodion*, then the number of days of the Afterfeast from 7 can be reduced to 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, and the reason for this - various services of the *Triodion*, with which it coincides. However, this reduction does not always take place in the middle of the *Triodion*, but only when the Apodosis of the Feast coincides with certain services of the *Triodion*, which are incompatible with the service of the Feast. Such are: Meatfare Saturday (of Souls), Meatfare Sunday, which is of the Last Judgment, Cheesefare Wednesday and Friday, which have a completely Lenten rule, and Monday of the 1st week of Lent, on which the day of 9 February can fall, and partially also Cheesefare Sunday. Generally one can establish such a rule: if Pascha falls on days from 8 April and earlier, and the *Triodion* - from 28 January and earlier, then the Apodosis of the Meeting will be 9 February, that is on the seventh day after the Feast. When in a given year the Apodosis of the Feast will be at its proper time, and earlier, when there will be no Apodosis at all, the following table, compiled according to the rules of Slavic menaia, will show.')

The reason that the Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos has a separate rule for Monday is that in this case the service of the Synaxis is combined with the service of the Sunday after the Nativity, namely of the Holy Kinsmen of God, King David, Joseph the Betrothed and James, the Brother of the Lord. If, therefore, the Synaxis falls on Monday, then the Sunday after the Nativity would fall on 1 January, that is already after the Apodosis of the Feast, which will be 31 December; therefore, according to the typikon, it is transferred back, to 26 December.          BACKUP had: 'EOF'
Line 3951: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 1.	Since the last boundary of the *Triodion* is 14 February, this feast always falls in the middle of the *Triodion*. If the *Triodion* is earlier, then this feast enters all the deeper into the *Triodion* and coincides with many *Triodion* services. Even more, this feast can coincide with other services, given in the *Triodion* from Wednesday of Meatfare Week to Tuesday of the 8th week of the *Triodion*, that is of the 4th of Great Lent, inclusive. The last boundary of the beginning of the *Triodion* is 14 February, and after subtracting from 14 February 13 days, which precede the beginning of the *Triodion*, 11 will remain, dividing which by 7, we will get in the quotient 1, with 4 in the remainder, that is one whole week and one not whole - the first four days; and since the first day of the first week is Sunday (for the *Triodion* begins on Sunday), then the first day of the second week will be Sunday, the second - Monday, the third - Tuesday, the fourth - Wednesday. And since the first Sunday of the *Triodion* is the Sunday of the Publican, the second - of the Prodigal [Son], the third - Meatfare, then the Wednesday on which the Finding falls will be Meatfare Wednesday (for in the Lenten *Triodion* the days of the week are named after the following Sunday), as the earliest boundary of this feast in relation to the *Triodion*. And that the last boundary of this feast in relation to the *Triodion* is Tuesday of the 4th week of Great Lent is proven thus. The first boundary of the *Triodion* is 11 January, from which to 24 February will be 45 days, dividing which by 7, we will get 6 whole weeks with a remainder of 3; but, since the first day of this remainder is Sunday, as is the first day of each of the 6 past weeks, it will be the 7th Sunday of the *Triodion*, and the second day will be Monday, the third - Tuesday of the 8th week of the *Triodion*, of the 4th of Great Lent.'

Line 100: BACKUP: '##### 2.	Neither Greek nor Slavonic rubrics give the form of the great or small prostration. However, according to custom it will be thus: he who makes a great prostration falls on his knees and touches the ground with his forehead; he who makes a small prostration does not fall on his knees, nor touches the ground with his forehead, but only crossing himself reaches the ground with his right hand, or only to the knees as the Synod of Lviv prescribes in Title V "On the Holy Liturgy", in the prayers before the iconostasis before the Proskomedia[^481]. We reach the ground with the right hand when we bow to the Holy Mysteries; only to the knees when we bow to holy icons, or at various supplications. However, our people in these parts do not have the custom, when bowing, to extend hands to the ground, or to the knees, but only crossing themselves to bow low before the Holy Mysteries, and higher - in other circumstances. We suppose, however, that at small Lenten prostrations we should reach the knees with the hand, for throughout the whole year at the Trisagion and at "O come, let us worship" we make prostrations, not reaching the knees with the hand[^482].'

Line 584: BACKUP: '##### 2.	Immediately after the Theotokion "O Theotokos, Thou Art the vine" at the 3rd Hour and, after the corresponding Theotokia, at the other two Hours, the rubrics prescribe the reading of the Four Gospels, which today among us is read only in cathedral, or conciliar, churches[^573]. At the 6th Hour we read the Gospel not immediately after the Theotokion, but after the conclusion of the Troparion of the Prophecy and the Paremia with its Prokimena. The reading of the Four Gospels covers all the Evangelists, that is Matthew, Mark and Luke in full, and John - only up to the "Passion of Christ", that is up to "Now is the Son of man glorified", Section 46, verse 13.32. All the Evangelists, taken together, are divided into 9 readings, according to the number of the three Hours (3, 6, 9) and three days (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday). Matthew is divided into 2 readings, Mark - into 2, John - into 2, and Luke - into 3. The first reading covers the first half of Matthew, the second - the second half of Matthew, the third - the first half of Mark, the fourth - the second half of Mark, the fifth - the first part of Luke, the sixth - the second part of Luke, the seventh - the third part of Luke, the eighth - the first half of John, the ninth - the second half of John. The rubric does not indicate where the first half of the three Evangelists and the first and second parts of Luke end. But since Matthew has 28 chapters, its half ends with the 14th chapter, Mark - 16 chapters, so its half ends with the 8th chapter, Luke - 24 chapters, so its first part ends with the 8th chapter, and the second - with the 16th. John, up to "Now is [the Son of man] glorified", has 12 chapters and part of the 13th chapter, therefore its half ends with the 6th chapter and part of the 7th.'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: '')

Line 199: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 2.	Neither Greek nor Slavonic rubrics give the form of the great or small prostration. However, according to custom it will be thus: he who makes a great prostration falls on his knees and touches the ground with his forehead; he who makes a small prostration does not fall on his knees, nor touches the ground with his forehead, but only crossing himself reaches the ground with his right hand, or only to the knees as the Synod of Lviv prescribes in Title V "On the Holy Liturgy", in the prayers before the iconostasis before the Proskomedia[^481]. We reach the ground with the right hand when we bow to the Holy Mysteries; only to the knees when we bow to holy icons, or at various supplications. However, our people in these parts do not have the custom, when bowing, to extend hands to the ground, or to the knees, but only crossing themselves to bow low before the Holy Mysteries, and higher - in other circumstances. We suppose, however, that at small Lenten prostrations we should reach the knees with the hand, for throughout the whole year at the Trisagion and at "O come, let us worship" we make prostrations, not reaching the knees with the hand[^482].'

         BACKUP had: 'The Priest, on one of the days preceding the feast, let him consecrate at the Liturgy two Lambs: one let him consume at Communion, and the other let him place in the tabernacle and keep until the day of the feast. On the day of the feast itself, after the Proskomedia, immediately before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy, after the censing of everything as usual by deacons (or by the Priest himself), the exposition of the Holy Mysteries takes place in the following way: the first deacon (who is on the right of the Priest) places the Gospel on the right side of the holy table, unlocks the artophorion and, having bowed low to the Holy Mysteries, takes from the artophorion the pyx, all bend their knees, and he places it on the folded antimension; if there be a monstrance, then he unlocks the pyx, takes from it the Lamb, not touching it with his fingers, but holding by the stand on which it lies, places it into the groove of the monstrance, locks it well, then places the pyx into the artophorion, bows before it and, having locked the artophorion, places the monstrance, turned with face side to the people, on the antimension and steps aside a little to the right side. The Priest puts incense into the censer, blesses it, saying: "Blessed is our God", and censes with both hands the Holy Mysteries three times, bowing His head at each censing. Then, having taken upon Himself with the help of the second deacon the omophorion, approaches the holy table and, having bowed low, with the help of the first Deacon takes with both hands with the omophorion the monstrance and, having turned it with the reverse side to himself, turns his right side to the people and sings solemnly and majestically the beginning of the first strophe: "O saving Victim", and all people continue to sing the same strophe. And again the Priest - the beginning of the second strophe: "To the One God in Trinity", and all sing the rest. The Priest signs the people crosswise with the Holy Mysteries, then goes in a semicircle from the southern side to the northern and, having returned by the northern to the altar, places the monstrance on the antimension, having turned it with the help of the Deacon with face side to the people. Then, having stepped aside a little to the left, descends before the steps of the altar so as not to turn his back to the Holy Mysteries, kneels and, having put aside the omophorion and having censed again three times the Holy Mysteries, as at the beginning, waits, kneeling, until the Deacon, having approached the middle of the altar and bowed low, places the Holy Mysteries on the tabernacle. Then the Priest, having ascended the steps, begins the Liturgy from "Blessed is the Kingdom", "O Heavenly King" and the rest. During the Liturgy the sacred ministers never turn their backs to the Holy Mysteries, as our Sluzhebnyky prescribe: "When (the Priest), according to the ritual prescriptions, has to turn to the people, he should not turn from the middle of the altar, so as not to turn his back to the Body of Christ, but, having bowed low and stepped aside a little to the left side, from this side turns to the people and, having turned again to the altar, bows low to the Body of Christ, and then, when the Priest has to make a full turn, as at 'Always, now and ever', when he turns with the Holy Mysteries, then he does not make a full turn, so as not to turn his back to the Body of Christ"[^662]. Let us add also that when the Priest or deacon goes out before the iconostasis for censing, he does not cense from the middle, nor turns his back to the Holy Mysteries, but stands a little on the side, the Priest - from the side of the Theotokos, and the deacons: one - from the side of the Savior, and the other - of the Theotokos.'

Line 1167: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 2.	Immediately after the Theotokion "O Theotokos, Thou Art the vine" at the 3rd Hour and, after the corresponding Theotokia, at the other two Hours, the rubrics prescribe the reading of the Four Gospels, which today among us is read only in cathedral, or conciliar, churches[^573]. At the 6th Hour we read the Gospel not immediately after the Theotokion, but after the conclusion of the Troparion of the Prophecy and the Paremia with its Prokimena. The reading of the Four Gospels covers all the Evangelists, that is Matthew, Mark and Luke in full, and John - only up to the "Passion of Christ", that is up to "Now is the Son of man glorified", Section 46, verse 13.32. All the Evangelists, taken together, are divided into 9 readings, according to the number of the three Hours (3, 6, 9) and three days (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday). Matthew is divided into 2 readings, Mark - into 2, John - into 2, and Luke - into 3. The first reading covers the first half of Matthew, the second - the second half of Matthew, the third - the first half of Mark, the fourth - the second half of Mark, the fifth - the first part of Luke, the sixth - the second part of Luke, the seventh - the third part of Luke, the eighth - the first half of John, the ninth - the second half of John. The rubric does not indicate where the first half of the three Evangelists and the first and second parts of Luke end. But since Matthew has 28 chapters, its half ends with the 14th chapter, Mark - 16 chapters, so its half ends with the 8th chapter, Luke - 24 chapters, so its first part ends with the 8th chapter, and the second - with the 16th. John, up to "Now is [the Son of man] glorified", has 12 chapters and part of the 13th chapter, therefore its half ends with the 6th chapter and part of the 7th.'

Line 1521: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 2.	BEGINNING OF MATINS. Immediately after the church doors are closed, the main priest, holding with his left hand the cross, and with his right - the censer and censing the church doors[^617], exclaims loudly: "Glory to the Holy" and the rest. The Choir responds: "Amen"; the Priest gives up the censer and sings loudly the troparion "Christ is risen", also all - the same, then the Priest the second time - the same and all - the same, and the third time the Priest - the same and all - the same, then the Priest in a high voice exclaims the verses, and all after each verse sing this troparion once[^618]. At the end the Priest, having sung in a higher voice the same troparion only up to "trampling down death by death" inclusive, opens the doors, and all finish: "and upon those in the tombs bestowing life" and again all bells ring, all enter the church[^619]. The Matins prayers at Resurrection Matins throughout the whole Bright Week are not recited, for they are connected with the Six Psalms, and since there will be no Six Psalms here, there will be no prayers. If it were necessary to recite the prayers, it should be indicated in the rubric where they should be recited, for during the verses "Let God arise", which take the place of the Six Psalms, it is not possible to recite them, for at this time the rubric orders the Priest to sing verses, and not to add prayers as well.'

Line 5: BACKUP: '##### 1. ABOUT THE EXPOSITION OF THE HOLY MYSTERIES ON THE HOLY TABLE'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: 'The temple rubrics used among us are of a double kind: some are borrowed from local Western Churches, which do not enter into the composition of our divine service, but are only added to it; others are natural to our divine service. Rubrics borrowed from Western Churches relate to the Holy Mysteries of the Eucharist, which are exposed on the holy table on the day of the temple feast and with which a procession takes place around the church. First, it befits us to provide the rubrics for the exposition and procession, and later - for the others.')

Line 21: BACKUP: '##### 1. GENERAL RUBRICS'
         CURRENT: (No heading at this line, current has: 'Before the dismissal of Vespers, all kneel, and the Deacon takes the Holy Gospel from the middle of the holy table and, having placed it on the right side, removes the Holy Mysteries from the skynia and places [Them] on the folded iliton. The Priest censes Them thrice with a bowing of the head and, having given away the censer, takes upon himself the omophorets [humeral veil], approaches the Holy Mysteries and, having bowed low, takes Them with both hands, with the help of the Deacon, turns right to the people, begins some pious hymn and goes out through the holy doors into the church; he enters under the baldachin and proceeds to the church doors, preceded by deacons with censers, who incessantly cense the Holy Mysteries from the sides; after them follow other priests in phelons, some - only in epitrachelia, with lighted candles in their hands, in two wings, likewise - the church brotherhood, afterwards - four girls with icons, banner-bearers and the cross-bearer. Under the sounds of bells, the procession goes out of the church and encircles it, beginning from its northern side, and returning from the southern side. When the Priest with the Holy Mysteries reaches the middle of the northern side, the procession stops, interrupts the singing, all kneel, and the Priest blesses all the present people with the Holy Mysteries four times, that is, first directly before himself, then - to the right side, then - behind and finally - to the left, saying each time in a quiet voice: "Save, O God, Thy people and bless Thine inheritance." Similarly it happens on the eastern, southern and western sides[^664]. After the blessing on the western side, the procession enters the church: first the Priest with the Holy Mysteries, other sacred ministers, then - the rest of the procession and the people. Then the Priest places the Holy Mysteries on the holy table, on the folded iliton, and, having laid aside the omophorets, kneels and censes the Holy Mysteries thrice. All kneel, and the Priest, together with other sacred ministers, sings the verses of the supplicatory hymn "Holy God." All the people repeat each of its verses. After the completion of the litiya, the Priest, having censed the Holy Mysteries thrice and having taken upon himself the omophorets, approaches the holy table and, having bowed low, takes the Holy Mysteries and, having turned right to the people, sings piously the verse of the hymn of St. Ambrose "Save Thy people, O Lord" twice, and the people repeat the same. The third time the Priest [sings]: "Save Thy people, O Lord, and bless Thine inheritance"; singing: "and bless," He blesses the people solemnly crosswise, making a half-turn from the right to the left side.')
Line 23: BACKUP: '##### 2.	The feast of a temple saint, even if of a lower rank, exceeds even a feast of a saint with a Vigil, primarily in that, when it falls on a Sunday, it includes at Matins before the Canon the Prokimenon, the Gospel, and the Sunday Sticheron [after the Gospel], exactly as a Feast of the Theotokos; also, the Gospel Sticheron is transferred from the "Praises" to the end of Matins. Besides this, if it falls on a weekday, it excludes at the Liturgy the Apostle and Gospel of the day, which is then read on the day before the feast. Finally, the temple feast of a saint has its Apodosis, which takes place on the very day of the feast at Vespers for the following day, with an Entrance, as on a Feast of the Lord. In this Apodosis at "Lord, I have cried," there will be 6 stichera: 3 of the temple and 3 of the daily saint; Glory: of the temple; Both now: Theotokion from the Sunday [Octoechos] (Dogmatic) according to the tone of the Doxastikon. After this he takes the chalice and, turning to the people, blesses them with the chalice, saying: "O God, save Thy people." Having placed the chalice on the holy table, He censes it with three swings, saying: "Be Thou exalted." Then He places the purificator under the small veil, with which the chalice is covered, and places the folded star-cover and the second small veil and aer on the holy diskos, makes a small bow, takes the holy chalice and, having turned to the holy doors, looking at the people, says quietly: "Blessed is our God"; after this exclaims: "Always, now and ever." Then He takes from the throne with His left hand the diskos and goes to the table of oblation, on which He leaves everything, and after a small bow returns to the holy table.'

Line 2013: CURRENT NEW HEADING: '##### 228. After the completion of the Hours and after the dismissal at the end of the Typika the holy doors are closed, the Priest and deacons make before the holy table three small bows each, saying: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner" and kiss the Holy Gospel, the edge of the holy table and the altar cross, as usual. After this the 1st deacon, having paid respect to the Priest, goes out through the northern doors and, having stood at his place before the holy doors, makes three small bows, saying nothing, after which he exclaims: "Bless, Master."'
